area: Autonomous Agent Loop Design (2024–2026): ReAct, Reflexion, Self-Refine, Plan-and-Solve, Tree-of-Thought, Completion Gating, Verifier-in-the-Loop, LLM-as-Judge, Stop Conditions

mechanisms.name: ReAct (Reason + Act) Loop
mechanisms.whatItIs: ReAct interleaves chain-of-thought reasoning steps with tool-invocation (action) steps in a tight perceive-reason-act cycle. The model emits a 'Thought:' trace, then an 'Action:', receives an 'Observation:', and repeats. The loop terminates when the model emits a terminal action or a configured turn limit is hit. It is the dominant backbone of production coding agents (SWE-agent, Claude Code, OpenHands) because it is simple, debuggable, and model-agnostic.
mechanisms.evidence: Yao et al. 2022 (arXiv:2210.03629). Claude Code design-space paper (arXiv:2604.14228) describes it as: 'The model generates reasoning and tool invocations, the harness executes actions, and results feed the next iteration.' SWE-agent runs 'a while not done loop' over this cycle.
mechanisms.applicability: pi-goal already uses this backbone. The leverage point is not replacing it but enriching what gets injected at each Observation step — specifically, the goal_state block, reflection summaries, and PRM course-correction signals (see PRM entry below).

mechanisms.name: Reflexion: Verbal Reinforcement via Episodic Memory
mechanisms.whatItIs: Reflexion (Shinn et al., NeurIPS 2023) adds three components on top of a ReAct actor: an Evaluator that scores each completed attempt (binary pass/fail or scalar), a Self-Reflection Model that generates a natural-language post-mortem when the attempt fails, and a persistent Episodic Memory Buffer that accumulates those reflections. On the next attempt, all prior reflections are prepended to the Actor's context as in-context examples. This creates a trial-and-error improvement curve without gradient updates or fine-tuning. On HumanEval coding tasks, Reflexion reached 91% with GPT-3.5, versus 68% without.
mechanisms.evidence: arXiv:2303.11366 (NeurIPS 2023). GitHub: noahshinn/reflexion. The three-component architecture (Actor/Evaluator/Self-Reflection) is described verbatim in the paper PDF fetched during this research.
mechanisms.applicability: After each agent run that hits the COMPLETION GATE but fails it, pi-goal could invoke a Self-Reflection step: prompt the model to write a short post-mortem ('What did I attempt? What was missing? What would I do differently?') and store it in SQLite alongside the goal. On the next retry, that reflection is injected into the mission system prompt as accumulated context, turning repeated failures into a gradient-free learning signal.

mechanisms.name: Self-Refine: Generate → Critique → Refine Loop
mechanisms.whatItIs: Self-Refine (Madaan et al., NeurIPS 2023, arXiv:2303.17651) uses the same model in three roles sequentially without any weight updates: (1) Generator produces an initial output; (2) Critic evaluates it against explicit criteria and writes natural-language feedback; (3) Refiner revises the output using the critique. The loop repeats until a stopping condition is met (no-improvement signal from the critic, or iteration budget). Averaged across seven diverse tasks, Self-Refine produced a 20% performance gain over single-shot generation. The key insight is that LLMs are more reliable as critics than as one-shot generators.
mechanisms.evidence: arXiv:2303.17651 (NeurIPS 2023). The paper reports 20% average improvement. The critique-then-refine pattern is also the foundation of the G-Eval LLM-as-judge framework (see that entry).
mechanisms.applicability: pi-goal's completion gate currently blocks stopping but does not refine the work. A Self-Refine loop could be inserted before the gate: after each major task completes, a dedicated 'Critic' turn (separate system prompt, explicit criteria: 'Does this implementation satisfy the goal? Are tests present? Are edge cases handled?') generates feedback that the agent consumes in a Refiner turn. The critic's criteria can be driven directly from the structured_evidence fields already in goal_complete.

mechanisms.name: Plan-and-Solve (PS+): Explicit Upfront Decomposition
mechanisms.whatItIs: Plan-and-Solve prompting (Wang et al., ACL 2023) instructs the model to first emit a complete plan decomposing the task into numbered subtasks before taking any actions. The PS+ variant adds the instruction to 'pay attention to calculations and relevant information' while planning, reducing errors from premature execution. It consistently outperforms zero-shot chain-of-thought and approaches few-shot CoT on reasoning benchmarks, with up to +8.0 percentage points on MultiArith. The mechanism works because upfront decomposition forces the model to surface ambiguities and dependencies before it can get lost in execution.
mechanisms.evidence: ResearchGate: 'Plan-and-Solve Prompting: Improving Zero-Shot Chain-of-Thought Reasoning by Large Language Models' (Wang et al., ACL 2023). Also described in Lilian Weng's survey at lilianweng.github.io/posts/2023-06-23-agent/.
mechanisms.applicability: When a new goal is set in pi-goal, the first LLM turn could be a Plan-and-Solve turn: the model is given the goal and instructed to produce a numbered breakdown of tasks before any tools are called. These tasks are then committed to the SQLite task list via goal_task. This is stronger than the current approach of letting tasks emerge implicitly, because it forces the model to confront scope upfront and the resulting task list can be used by the COMPLETION GATE as a checklist.

mechanisms.name: Tree-of-Thought / LATS / CodeTree: Search-Based Planning with Critic-Guided Pruning
mechanisms.whatItIs: Tree-of-Thought (Yao et al. 2023) generalizes chain-of-thought into a tree where each node is an intermediate reasoning state, explored via BFS or DFS. Language Agent Tree Search (LATS, Zhou et al., ICML 2024) unifies this with ReAct and reflection, using MCTS with an LLM-as-value-function to guide search. CodeTree (Li et al., NAACL 2025, arXiv:2411.04329) applies this specifically to code generation with four specialized agents: a Thinker (strategy generation), Solver (code generation), Debugger (iterative refinement), and Critic (scoring and termination). The Critic executes three actions at each node: Refine (generate reflections), Abort (prune and backtrack), or Accept (terminate). CodeTree achieved 95.1% on HumanEval and 31.9% on SWE-bench with GPT-4o.
mechanisms.evidence: arXiv:2411.04329 (NAACL 2025). LATS repo: github.com/lapisrocks/LanguageAgentTreeSearch (ICML 2024). The Thinker/Solver/Debugger/Critic architecture and Refine/Abort/Accept termination logic were verified by fetching the CodeTree HTML paper.
mechanisms.applicability: For complex goals, pi-goal could implement a lightweight CodeTree-style exploration: the first turn generates N alternative strategies (Thinker), the agent executes the most promising one (Solver), tests determine if it passes (Critic signal), and if not, a Debugger turn refines rather than restarting. The Critic's Accept/Abort decision maps directly onto pi-goal's completion gate: Accept triggers goal_complete, Abort reinjects the task with a strategy-switch directive.

mechanisms.name: Process Reward Model (PRM) for In-Loop Course Correction
mechanisms.whatItIs: Process Reward Models assign scalar scores to intermediate agent steps rather than only to final outcomes. In the context of coding agents, 'Act Like You're Paying for This' (arXiv:2509.02360, 2025) built a PRM that monitors a sliding window of the last 8 agent steps against the original problem description, classifying errors into three families: Specification Errors (task violation, repetition, termination unawareness), Reasoning Errors (misidentification, hallucination, wrong tool), and Coordination Errors (goal deviation, context failures, verification failures). Every 5 steps the PRM injects natural-language corrective guidance. Using Claude Sonnet-4 as the PRM on top of SWE-agent-LM-32B raised SWE-bench Verified resolution from 40.0% to 50.6% (+10.6 pp) at a cost of $23.20 per additional success.
mechanisms.evidence: arXiv:2509.02360 (September 2025), fetched and verified. Three error families, k=8 sliding window, n=5 step frequency, and 10.6 pp improvement on SWE-bench Verified are all directly from the paper.
mechanisms.applicability: pi-goal's tool_call/tool_result hooks provide exactly the hook point needed. Every 5 tool invocations, pi-goal could run a lightweight PRM check: compare the last N tool calls against the current goal and task list, classify against the three error families, and if Specification or Coordination errors are detected, inject a corrective message before the next LLM call. This does not require training a reward model — the check can be done with a strong LLM using the taxonomy as a rubric (a zero-shot PRM).

mechanisms.name: LLM-as-Judge with Structured Rubrics (G-Eval / DAG Scoring)
mechanisms.whatItIs: LLM-as-Judge uses a separate (often stronger) model to evaluate agent outputs against explicit criteria. G-Eval (Liu et al.) stabilizes this by having the judge first generate evaluation steps from the criterion using chain-of-thought, then use those steps to score. The DAG variant structures evaluation as a decision tree of binary checks, enabling cascading verification (e.g., 'Do tests exist? -> Do they pass? -> Is coverage above threshold?'). Reliability best practices include: few-shot examples (+12.5% consistency for GPT-4), token-probability normalization across multiple scoring runs, and position/order randomization to counteract bias. A key finding is that LLMs are more reliable as comparative judges than as absolute scorers, motivating pairwise completion evaluation.
mechanisms.evidence: Confident AI blog (confident-ai.com/blog/why-llm-as-a-judge-is-the-best-llm-evaluation-method) — G-Eval, DAG scoring, and reliability techniques verified by fetching. arXiv:2411.16594 'From Generation to Judgment: Opportunities and Challenges of LLM-as-a-Judge'. arXiv:2601.14691 'Gaming the Judge' identifies adversarial vulnerabilities in chain-of-thought judges.
mechanisms.applicability: pi-goal's completion gate currently uses structured_evidence fields as a checklist. This can be upgraded to a G-Eval-style judge: a separate model turn with a rubric that maps directly to goal requirements (requirements_covered, verifications_run, task_evidence, shortcuts_considered), generates chain-of-thought reasoning for each dimension, then scores 1-5. A score below threshold blocks goal_complete and the reasoning is injected back as Reflexion-style feedback. The DAG pattern is particularly useful: 'Did tests run? -> Did they pass? -> Were edge cases addressed?' gives deterministic binary gates before the subjective quality score.

mechanisms.name: Stop-Hook / Completion Gate with Hard Circuit Breakers
mechanisms.whatItIs: Stop-condition design in 2025-2026 practitioner literature converges on a layered pattern: (1) a Stop Hook intercepts every agent exit attempt and validates objective completion criteria (tests green, type checks clean, coverage above threshold) before allowing termination; (2) a separate evaluator model (faster/cheaper) grades the work after each turn and only clears the loop when it passes; (3) hard circuit breakers — max turn count, token budget, no-progress detection (output unchanged across N iterations) — prevent infinite loops. The Ralph Loop (Geoffrey Huntley, July 2025) externalizes all state to the filesystem (TODO files, git history, codebase) so that context can be reset mid-loop without information loss. Claude Code's /goal primitive (v2.1.139, May 2026) implements a native stop-hook loop with a separate fast model grading after every turn.
mechanisms.evidence: datasciencedojo.com/blog/agentic-loops-explained (2026 guide) — Stop Hook, evaluator model, circuit breakers, and Ralph Loop all described; fetched and verified. arXiv:2604.14228 (Claude Code design space) — five distinct stop conditions: no tool use, maxTurns, context overflow, hook_stopped_continuation, abortController.
mechanisms.applicability: pi-goal's COMPLETION GATE is the right architectural choice and is ahead of most frameworks. The upgrades are: (a) add a no-progress circuit breaker — if the same files are unchanged after 3 consecutive tool-call cycles, inject a 'you appear to be stuck' message; (b) replace the single gate at agent_end with periodic lightweight checks every K turns using a fast model (e.g., haiku-class) so failures are caught early rather than at the end; (c) store all task state in the SQLite DB so context compaction never loses goal progress.

mapsToPiGoal:
1. REPLACE THE SINGLE END-GATE WITH A PERIODIC PRM-STYLE MONITOR: The most impactful single change is moving from one completion check at agent_end to a periodic in-loop monitor every 5 turns. Use the three-family error taxonomy from arXiv:2509.02360 (Specification/Reasoning/Coordination errors) as a zero-shot rubric: pass the last N tool_call/tool_result pairs plus the active goal and task list to a fast model every 5 steps. This catches goal drift and repetition loops early, before 30 turns of wasted compute, and injects corrective guidance exactly as the PRM paper demonstrated (+10.6 pp on SWE-bench). pi-goal's tool_result hook is the natural injection point.

2. ADD REFLEXION-STYLE FAILURE MEMORY TO THE COMPLETION GATE: When a goal attempt fails the gate, invoke a Self-Reflection turn that writes a structured post-mortem into SQLite (what was tried, what was missing, what the next attempt should do differently). On retry, prepend all stored reflections to the mission system prompt. This converts repeated failures into a gradient-free improvement signal — the mechanism demonstrated 91% vs 68% on HumanEval — and makes the gate an active improvement driver rather than just a blocker. The structured_evidence fields in goal_complete already give the reflection model a scaffold to work from.

3. UPGRADE THE COMPLETION GATE TO A G-EVAL DAG JUDGE: Replace the current boolean gate with a two-stage G-Eval judge: first a DAG of binary deterministic checks (did tests run? did they pass? were all tasks marked done?), then a chain-of-thought rubric scoring each structured_evidence dimension on a 1-5 scale. The DAG stage catches objective failures cheaply; the rubric stage catches quality gaps. The judge's reasoning, not just its verdict, is injected back as Reflexion feedback when it blocks. Use a separate model invocation (haiku-class for cost) to avoid the main agent judging its own work, which the 'Gaming the Judge' paper (arXiv:2601.14691) shows is unreliable.

area: Factory.ai Droid Missions — Long-Running Task Model

mechanisms.name: Validation Contract as Pre-Implementation Completion Oracle
mechanisms.whatItIs: Before any feature is written, the orchestrator creates a validation-contract.md containing a finite, numbered set of behavioral assertions (e.g., VAL-AUTH-001). Each assertion has a stable ID, a short title, a semantic unambiguous pass/fail behavioral description, and an explicit evidence-requirements field (screenshots, exit codes, network calls, terminal output). A parallel validation-state.json tracks each ID's status as pending/passed/failed/blocked. The mission CANNOT declare completion until ALL assertions show 'passed'. No assertion may appear in more than one feature's 'fulfills' array — every assertion has a single responsible feature. The contract is written before features.json, enforcing that success criteria precede implementation.
mechanisms.evidence: Factory.ai missions-architecture page: 'Finite checklist of testable behavioral assertions defining completion... validation contract before implementation begins.' Reverse-engineered gist (https://gist.github.com/V1ki/356b121038722ebf32b5aac85482c113): 'ALL assertions must be passed before declaring success'; features.json schema shows 'fulfills' array of VAL-IDs; validation-state.json schema: {assertions: {VAL-ID: {status: pending|passed|failed|blocked}}}.
mechanisms.applicability: pi-goal's completion gate currently requires the agent to self-report structured evidence fields. Replacing or augmenting that with a pre-written validation contract — authored during goal-setting, not at completion — would make the gate deterministic. Each goal task could map to one or more VAL-IDs, and the goal_complete tool would be blocked unless all mapped IDs are passed. The extension can persist this contract in SQLite alongside the existing goal+tasks schema.

mechanisms.name: Orchestrator/Worker Role Separation with Fresh Contexts
mechanisms.whatItIs: The orchestrator holds the plan and drives sequencing but never accumulates granular implementation context. Each feature is handed to a freshly spawned worker session with a narrowly scoped context: just its feature spec, the AGENTS.md conventions, and the shared artifact files. Workers cannot spawn sub-agents, ask the user questions, or propose missions — they can only read/write/execute code. The orchestrator synthesises worker handoffs and decides whether to proceed, create fix features, or block. This prevents the 'context accumulation' failure mode where a long-running single agent degrades in quality.
mechanisms.evidence: missions-architecture page: 'agents are highly reactive to their context... model performance degrades when contexts accumulate irrelevant information.' Gist: 'Implementation workers... struggle with ambiguity... Workers cannot spawn sub-agents, ask users questions, or propose missions.' features.json 'preconditions' and 'expectedBehavior' fields are the worker's entire spec.
mechanisms.applicability: pi-goal could implement a lightweight version: for large goals, the extension spawns sub-sessions (pi supports fork/spawn sessions in the extension API) for each task, passing only the task spec + relevant context messages, then synthesises results. The goal_state injection each turn already serves an orchestrator-like role; this would extend it to actually partition work rather than just track it.

mechanisms.name: features.json — Ordered Feature Queue with Explicit Preconditions and fulfills Pointers
mechanisms.whatItIs: features.json is a structured, ordered array — the next pending feature is always index 0. Each entry carries: id, description, skillName (which worker type to use), milestone (grouping), preconditions (array of strings that must be true before work starts), expectedBehavior (success definition), verificationSteps (how to test), fulfills (which VAL-IDs this feature satisfies), and status (pending/completed/cancelled). The orchestrator never decides execution order at runtime; it was fixed at planning time. The system 'pre-assigns a feature to the worker' — the worker has no choice about what to work on.
mechanisms.evidence: Gist reverse-engineering: full features.json schema with all field names listed. Factory docs: 'features are executed in array order — the topmost pending feature runs next.'
mechanisms.applicability: pi-goal's goal_task todo tool is currently unstructured. Enriching it with a fulfills field linking tasks to validation-contract assertions, plus verificationSteps per task, would give the goal_complete gate machine-checkable evidence requirements. The extension could enforce that a task cannot be marked complete unless its verificationSteps exit codes pass, which are run via the exec API.

mechanisms.name: Three-Tool Mission Control Protocol (ProposeMission / StartMissionRun / DismissHandoffItems)
mechanisms.whatItIs: The orchestrator is constrained to exactly three mission-management tools. ProposeMission (required fields: title, proposal) presents the decomposed plan for user review before any execution — the plan is never assumed, always confirmed. StartMissionRun blocks until worker handoffs return, preventing the orchestrator from taking shortcuts. DismissHandoffItems requires a typed dismissal (discovered_issue, critical_context, incomplete_work), the source feature ID, a summary, and a justification of at least 20 characters — making it costly and auditable to ignore surfaced work. Tech debt dismissal specifically requires citing an existing tracking feature or a reason it will never need fixing.
mechanisms.evidence: Gist reverse-engineering: exact tool schemas with required/optional fields and enumerated types. 'DismissHandoffItems... should be used sparingly... Tech debt dismissal requires citing an existing tracking feature.'
mechanisms.applicability: pi-goal's goal_complete tool already enforces structured-evidence fields as an audit. The DismissHandoffItems pattern is directly applicable: rather than letting the agent silently skip a task or sub-requirement, any skip requires a typed justification (enum: out_of_scope, deferred, known_limitation) with a minimum-length reason. This maps to extending goal_complete's required fields with a dismissed_items array using the same pattern.

mechanisms.name: TDD Red-Green Loop as a Deterministic Steering Mechanism
mechanisms.whatItIs: A dedicated test-writer sub-agent converts a spec into a failing test suite before any implementation occurs. The coding agent's only exit condition is a zero exit code from the test suite — 'specs define commands and pass/fail conditions; no fuzzy completion logic.' Every phase must produce a file or exit code (never rely on chat assertions). The orchestrator never trusts chat output; only exit codes and logged outputs count. This makes completion binary and removes the agent's ability to self-certify.
mechanisms.evidence: Medium article (Silas Schuettel): 'Confirm a non-zero exit. Capture file paths, failing assertions, and exit code... coding-agent cannot proceed until validation commands succeed with zero exit codes.' Factory missions-architecture: 'file-based validation where every phase must produce a file or exit code.'
mechanisms.applicability: pi-goal's completion gate currently relies on the agent calling goal_complete with self-reported evidence. The extension could instead run shell commands (via the exec API) as part of the gate — linting, type-checking, and test suite execution — and block goal_complete unless those commands exit 0. The .factory/services.yaml pattern (commands: {typecheck, build, test, lint}) could be mirrored in a pi-goal config file that the extension reads to know what validation commands to run.

mechanisms.name: Milestone-Gated Dual Validation (Scrutiny + Black-Box User-Testing)
mechanisms.whatItIs: At each milestone boundary, two sequential validator agents run independently. The scrutiny validator reviews implementation quality — tests, lint, code inspection. The user-testing validator exercises the system as a black box against the behavioral assertions in the validation contract, without seeing the implementation. Validators cannot skip failures without an auditable justification in synthesis.json. If validators surface issues, the orchestrator creates targeted 'fix features' and runs another implementation-validation cycle. The milestone only advances when both validators pass.
mechanisms.evidence: missions-architecture page: 'scrutiny validators review implementation quality, while user-testing validators exercise the system as a black box against behavioral assertions.' Gist: 'ALL assertions must be passed before declaring success; override requires auditable trail justification in synthesis.json.' Example: 81 issues surfaced across 6 milestones, producing 21 fix features on the Slack clone mission.
mechanisms.applicability: pi-goal could introduce a milestone concept into goal tasks — when a milestone group completes, the extension triggers a validator turn (a fork/spawn session in the pi API) with a black-box prompt that checks observable behavior against the validation contract, rather than the implementing agent self-checking. The COMPLETION GATE already forces an additional turn; this would make that turn structurally separate from the implementing agent.

mechanisms.name: Autonomy Level Tiers with Progressive Trust
mechanisms.whatItIs: Factory exposes three explicit autonomy levels: Low (file edits permitted automatically, every other action requires approval), Medium (reversible commands run without prompting, irreversible ones pause for approval), and High (full automation including non-easily-reversible commands). Users are instructed to 'start with low autonomy and work your way up as trust builds.' Each level is a persistent session setting, not a per-command choice. This gives users a calibration mechanism for how much the agent self-steers versus pauses.
mechanisms.evidence: Factory.ai Droid autonomy level docs (via Sid Bharath guide and Factory search results): 'Low: allow file edits but approve every other change. Medium: Droid handles reversible changes automatically, asks for risky ones. High: full autonomy.' Factory docs: 'Start with low autonomy.'
mechanisms.applicability: pi-goal's tool_call/tool_result hooks already intercept every tool call. The extension could expose an autonomy level setting for the goal that gates which tool calls are allowed to proceed without surfacing to the user for approval. Medium autonomy could mean: file reads/writes pass, shell commands with side effects (npm install, git push, database migrations) pause. This is directly implementable via the extension's tool_call hook.

mechanisms.name: Agent Readiness Framework — Repo Infrastructure as a Prerequisite, Not an Afterthought
mechanisms.whatItIs: Factory evaluates repositories across eight pillars (style/validation, build, testing, documentation, dev environment, code quality, observability, security) against 60+ binary criteria. Level 3 ('Standardized') requires E2E tests, maintained docs, security scanning, and observability — and is the target before running autonomous agents. Fast feedback loops (pre-commit hooks, local linting) are treated as mandatory infrastructure: 'missing pre-commit hooks force agents to wait for CI feedback instead of receiving immediate validation.' Repos must pass 80% of criteria at a level plus all prior levels before advancing.
mechanisms.evidence: factory.ai/news/agent-readiness: 'fast feedback and clear instructions will make any agent dramatically more effective.' The /readiness-report command uses LLM-evaluated binary checks on 60+ criteria. Level 3 criteria: clear processes, E2E tests, maintained docs, security scanning, observability.
mechanisms.applicability: pi-goal could add a readiness check as part of goal initialisation — before the agent starts work, the extension runs a lightweight check (does a test command exist in package.json/Makefile? is there a lint config? is there a AGENTS.md or CLAUDE.md?) and injects a readiness warning into the system prompt if gaps are found. This sets realistic expectations and primes the agent to establish missing infrastructure as a first task.

mapsToPiGoal: 1. Replace self-reported completion with a pre-authored validation contract: at goal-setting time (not at goal_complete time), author a validation-contract.md with numbered behavioral assertions and evidence requirements, persist it in SQLite alongside the goal, and block the COMPLETION GATE unless every assertion's status in validation-state.json is 'passed' — this makes the existing audit fields in goal_complete machine-checkable rather than agent-narrated. 2. Instrument the completion gate with exec-based validation commands: mirror the .factory/services.yaml pattern in a pi-goal config (test, lint, typecheck commands), run them via the extension's exec API inside the gate, and require zero exit codes before goal_complete is accepted — eliminating fuzzy self-certification and making the gate deterministic. 3. Enforce auditable dismissals for skipped requirements: extend goal_complete's required structured-evidence fields with a dismissed_items array matching Factory's DismissHandoffItems schema (type enum, source task ID, justification of minimum 20 chars) so that any requirement the agent skips is explicitly typed and justified rather than silently omitted, creating an audit trail directly inside the existing SQLite persistence layer.

area: OpenAI Codex CLI / Codex Agent and AGENTS.md Convention

mechanisms.name: AGENTS.md Hierarchical Instruction Loading
mechanisms.whatItIs: AGENTS.md is an open, vendor-neutral markdown file placed at project root (and optionally in subdirectories or ~/.codex/) that gives any compatible coding agent persistent, session-independent guidance. Codex reads it before doing any work by walking from the global ~/.codex/ directory down to the current working directory, concatenating files from root downward with closer files overriding earlier ones. An AGENTS.override.md at any level can wholesale replace parent guidance. Combined size is capped at 32 KiB by default (tunable via project_doc_max_bytes). The file is intentionally tool-agnostic plain markdown with no required fields—its value comes entirely from developer-curated content, not schema enforcement. Research cited by asdlc.io shows that LLM-generated AGENTS.md content actually reduces agent task success while raising inference cost by over 20%, so human curation is load-bearing.
mechanisms.evidence: OpenAI official docs at https://developers.openai.com/codex/guides/agents-md: 'Codex reads AGENTS.md files before doing any work' and 'Codex builds an instruction chain when it starts.' asdlc.io spec at https://asdlc.io/practices/agents-md-spec/ documents the 5-section canonical structure (Mission, Toolchain Registry, Judgment Boundaries, Personas Registry, Context Map) and the research finding on LLM-generated content degrading performance. The openai/codex repo's own AGENTS.md at https://github.com/openai/codex/blob/main/AGENTS.md demonstrates Rust crate naming, test-module layout, async trait patterns, code review change-size caps (800 lines non-mechanical, 500 lines complex logic), and snapshot test requirements.
mechanisms.applicability: Pi-goal can write an AGENTS.md (or inject its content into the session context) at goal-set time, encoding the current goal's acceptance criteria, forbidden scope, required test/lint commands, and review checklist. The three-tier NEVER/ASK/ALWAYS judgment-boundary pattern maps directly to pi's tool_call hook: the extension can enforce NEVER rules as hard blocks, ASK rules as approval gates, and ALWAYS rules as mandatory pre-completion steps. Keeping the injected content under ~2 KB and human-structured (not LLM-generated) maximises its steering signal.

mechanisms.name: PLANS.md / ExecPlan Living-Document Pattern
mechanisms.whatItIs: For multi-hour or multi-step tasks, Codex uses a trio of markdown files: Prompt.md (frozen spec with goals, constraints, deliverables), Plan.md (milestone list, each small enough to complete and verify in one loop), and Implement.md (execution instructions emphasising scope discipline). The plan itself is treated as a living document with four mandatory evolving sections: Progress (timestamped checkboxes), Surprises & Discoveries (unexpected findings), Decision Log (course corrections with rationale and timestamps), and Outcomes & Retrospective. Steps are written idempotently so they can re-run without damage if execution halts mid-milestone. Each milestone specifies a purpose statement, concrete commands, expected observable results, and acceptance criteria. The agent updates these sections at every stopping point.
mechanisms.evidence: OpenAI developer cookbook at https://developers.openai.com/cookbook/articles/codex_exec_plans describes ExecPlan format requirements and living-document principles. The 'run long-horizon tasks' blog post at https://developers.openai.com/blog/run-long-horizon-tasks-with-codex confirms the Prompt/Plan/Implement.md three-file pattern and milestone-based structure with per-milestone verification before proceeding.
mechanisms.applicability: Pi-goal currently stores tasks in SQLite and injects a goal_state reminder. Adding a PLANS.md-style living document—written to disk at goal-set time and updated after each task transition—would give the agent a self-contained resumable artifact. The Progress section with timestamped checkboxes could directly feed pi's task completion evidence fields. The Decision Log pattern is the equivalent of pi's 'shortcuts considered' evidence field: capturing why a shortcut was or was not taken makes the audit trail legible.

mechanisms.name: Observable-Outcome Completion Criteria (Evidence-Based, Not Belief-Based)
mechanisms.whatItIs: Codex's /goal command implements completion as an evidence audit, not model belief. A goal must specify a verification surface (tests, benchmarks, command outputs, generated artifacts), and the model cannot mark the goal complete without demonstrating that verification surface confirms success. Goals include six mandatory components: outcome, verification surface, constraints (what must not regress), boundaries (files/tools allowed), iteration policy (what to do between attempts), and a blocked-stop condition (when to halt and report rather than continue). The cookbook example pattern is: 'Reduce p95 latency below 120 ms, verified by checkout benchmark, while keeping correctness suite green. Use only checkout service. Between iterations, record changes and next experiments. If blocked, report attempted paths, evidence, and needed input.'
mechanisms.evidence: OpenAI developer cookbook at https://developers.openai.com/cookbook/examples/codex/using_goals_in_codex: 'Completion is evidence-based, not model-belief-based. Codex must inspect concrete evidence: Files changed, Command outputs, Test results, Benchmark metrics, Generated artifacts. The model cannot mark a Goal complete without demonstrating that the objective's verification surface confirms success.' Codex prompting guide at https://developers.openai.com/cookbook/examples/gpt-5/codex_prompting_guide: 'Plans guide your edits; the deliverable is working code. Plan closure requires reconciling every previously stated intention/TODO/plan, marking each as Done, Blocked, or Cancelled.'
mechanisms.applicability: Pi's existing completion gate already blocks stopping until goal_complete is called with structured evidence fields. The six-component goal schema from Codex maps tightly onto pi's existing fields (requirements covered → outcome + constraints, verifications run → verification surface, task evidence → observable outcomes, shortcuts considered → iteration policy + blocked-stop condition). Pi could adopt the explicit 'blocked stop condition' as a seventh required evidence field: forcing the agent to either present passing verification output or declare a specific blocking fact, eliminating vague 'I tried my best' completions.

mechanisms.name: Codex-1 Reinforcement Learning on Test-Pass Signal
mechanisms.whatItIs: Codex-1, the model powering Codex Cloud (released May 2025), is a version of OpenAI's o3 reasoning model fine-tuned via reinforcement learning on real-world software engineering tasks. The training reward signal is test passage: the model was trained to iteratively run tests until they pass, internalizing test-driven iteration as a core behavioral prior. This means the model's natural completion heuristic is 'tests are green,' not 'I believe I am done.' It also learned to mirror human-style code and PR conventions through the same RL process.
mechanisms.evidence: OpenAI introducing-codex page at https://openai.com/index/introducing-codex/ and the codex system card (May 2025) at https://cdn.openai.com/pdf/8df7697b-c1b2-4222-be00-1fd3298f351d/codex_system_card.pdf: model 'trained using reinforcement learning on real-world coding tasks...to iteratively run tests until passing results are achieved.' Also confirmed in Wikipedia summary of Codex (AI agent).
mechanisms.applicability: Because the underlying model has test-pass as a trained behavioral prior, pi-goal can exploit this by ensuring the goal_state reminder always includes the exact test and lint commands to run. If pi's goal_complete tool requires the agent to paste actual test output as evidence, the model's RL training creates alignment: the model will naturally run tests before claiming completion because that is what it was rewarded for. Pi should make test commands prominent and early in every injected context message, not buried in the task list.

mechanisms.name: Approval Policy Layered Over OS Sandbox for Scope Enforcement
mechanisms.whatItIs: Codex CLI enforces scope at two independent layers. The first is an OS-level sandbox (macOS: Seatbelt/sandbox-exec; Linux: bwrap + seccomp; Windows: native sandbox) that physically prevents the agent from writing outside the workspace or accessing the network. The second is an approval policy layer (on-request, untrusted, never) that determines when the agent must pause and ask before acting, independent of whether the OS would allow the action. The agent halts before attempting to: modify files outside the workspace, access the network when disabled, run commands flagged as untrusted or potentially destructive, access protected paths (.git, .agents, .codex), or invoke MCP tools advertising side effects. An optional auto-review mode routes approval requests through a reviewer subagent that checks for data exfiltration, credential probing, and destructive patterns before execution proceeds.
mechanisms.evidence: Official Codex sandbox docs at https://developers.openai.com/codex/concepts/sandboxing and approval/security docs at https://developers.openai.com/codex/agent-approvals-security detail the three sandbox modes (read-only, workspace-write, danger-full-access) paired with three approval policies. The auto-review reviewer agent mechanism is described in the approval docs.
mechanisms.applicability: Pi's tool_call hook already intercepts calls before execution. The two-layer pattern maps directly: pi can implement a 'sandbox layer' by blocking tool calls touching paths outside the goal's declared file scope, and an 'approval layer' by requiring confirmation before any tool with declared side effects (network, package install, git push). Crucially, the auto-review pattern—routing flagged calls through a second agent before execution—is directly achievable in pi via fork/spawn session to a reviewer instance, without blocking the primary agent's context.

mechanisms.name: Plan Mode with Modal Intent Signal and Clarifying-Question Phase
mechanisms.whatItIs: Codex supports a distinct plan mode (toggled via /plan or Shift+Tab) where the agent gathers context and asks clarifying questions before writing any code. The community discussion (GitHub Discussion #7355) found strong consensus that a hard modal switch 'clearly signals intent to the model' and prevents accidental code changes during planning. Internal OpenAI AGENTS.md structure distinguishes lightweight 'plans' (sketches) from formal 'specs' (including overview, RFC 2119 modal-verb requirements—MUST/SHOULD/MAY—and design sections). The plan-generation skill stores persistent plans in ~/.codex/plans/ for version control. The prompting guide explicitly states to skip the planning tool for the easiest ~25% of tasks, use it for complex multi-step work, and never end an interaction with only a plan—the deliverable is working code.
mechanisms.evidence: GitHub Discussion #7355 at https://github.com/openai/codex/discussions/7355: 'a hard modal switch clearly signals intent to the model' and discussion of persistent plan storage. OpenAI best practices at https://developers.openai.com/codex/learn/best-practices: 'Plan Mode: Toggle with /plan or Shift+Tab to let Codex gather context and ask clarifying questions before implementation.' Prompting guide at https://developers.openai.com/cookbook/examples/gpt-5/codex_prompting_guide: 'Skip using the planning tool for roughly the easiest 25%' and 'never end the interaction with only a plan.'
mechanisms.applicability: Pi-goal already has a goal-set phase that could incorporate a mandatory planning turn before task execution begins. Adding an explicit planning gate—where the agent must produce a structured plan (with RFC 2119 MUST/SHOULD/MAY verbs) and receive approval before any file edits—would reduce scope drift on complex goals. Pi's goal_task todo tool could be gated: tasks cannot be created after the planning phase closes, enforcing upfront scope rather than scope creep during execution.

mechanisms.name: Explorer/Worker/Orchestrator Subagent Role Separation
mechanisms.whatItIs: Codex's subagent system (shipped March 2026) defines three named roles: explorer (read-only, context gathering, safe parallelization), worker (read-write, execution, sandboxed to a task-specific output directory), and default/orchestrator (coordinates workers, synthesizes results). Up to six subagents run concurrently. Workers are isolated with per-task write directories (outputs/<task_id>/) and explicit forbid-glob patterns preventing cross-task file conflicts. The orchestrator runs a supervisor phase first (generating a machine-readable task plan), then fans out to workers. File-based task queues (JSONL with fields: id, role, cwd, message, context_files, explicit allowlist, deps for ordering) are the coordination mechanism. Dependencies between tasks are tracked via a deps field enabling sequential ordering when needed.
mechanisms.evidence: GitHub Discussion #3898 at https://github.com/openai/codex/discussions/3898 describes the planner-first architecture with file-based JSONL queues and xargs-P parallelization. Medium article by Rick Hightower confirms the three-role model (explorer/worker/default) with up to six concurrent subagents as the March 2026 release. Web search results from https://medium.com/@richardhightower/codex-gets-subagents confirm 'Codex now features three roles: explorer for read-only analysis, worker for read-write execution, and default for general tasks.'
mechanisms.applicability: Pi's fork/spawn session capability is the direct primitive for this pattern. For a pi-goal task like 'implement feature X with tests,' a high-quality workflow would be: (1) spawn an explorer session to read current codebase and produce a task plan, (2) spawn one worker per independent task with its own sandboxed scope, (3) use the orchestrator session to merge results and run the completion gate. The pi extension could implement the explorer role as a specialized read-only session that feeds structured task breakdown back to the goal planner before execution starts, directly improving task breakdown quality.

mechanisms.name: AGENTS.md Review Guidelines as Mechanical Pre-Completion Checklist
mechanisms.whatItIs: A specific section of AGENTS.md called '## Review guidelines' is automatically used by Codex as its checklist when reviewing pull requests or preparing for completion. The guidance states that items in this section 'should be specific and mechanical, not qualitative.' Examples: 'Run npm test && npm run lint && npm run build before marking complete' rather than 'write good code.' Review findings can carry priority levels 0–3 (P0 = critical, P3 = suggestion), and a hook that blocks on any P0 finding provides a CI-style gate locally. The --output-schema flag forces structured JSON output from review passes, enabling programmatic parsing of review findings. Additionally, AGENTS.md can specify 'programmatic checks Codex will attempt to run before finishing a task'—these are listed as advisory but form a strong behavioral prior given the model's RL training.
mechanisms.evidence: Codex CLI best-practices doc at https://developers.openai.com/codex/learn/best-practices: 'Ask it to create tests when needed, run the relevant checks, confirm the result, and review the work before you accept it.' Web search results from Verdent Guides and Educative.io confirm the '## Review guidelines' section is specifically parsed by Codex for PR review checklists, with items being 'specific and mechanical.' Priority 0–3 system and --output-schema flag for programmatic review output described in search results.
mechanisms.applicability: Pi's goal_complete tool currently requires structured evidence fields filled by the agent. A '## Review guidelines' equivalent injected into the goal_state context before every turn—listing specific mechanical checks (e.g., 'pytest must pass with exit code 0', 'ruff check must show no errors', 'all acceptance criteria in the goal must be explicitly addressed')—would align the model's pre-completion self-check with pi's gate requirements. Pi could parse the agent's review output for P0 items and automatically block goal_complete if any P0 finding is present, without requiring human review.

mapsToPiGoal:
1. Adopt the six-component goal schema (outcome, verification surface, constraints, boundaries, iteration policy, blocked-stop condition) as the structured input to pi's goal_set command, and require the agent to map every component to concrete evidence before goal_complete is accepted. This directly raises audit quality by eliminating belief-based completion claims. The 'blocked-stop condition' component is the highest-leverage addition: it forces the agent to either present passing command output or name a specific blocking fact, closing the 'I tried my best' escape hatch that currently degrades output quality.

2. Inject a mechanical '## Review guidelines' checklist into every goal_state context message—listing exact commands (test runner, linter, type checker) with expected exit codes as acceptance criteria—and parse the agent's pre-completion review output for P0 (critical) findings using pi's tool_result hook. Block goal_complete automatically if any P0 finding is present. This exploits the codex-1 model's RL-trained behavioral prior of running tests before completion, aligning the model's internalized reward signal with pi's external gate.

3. Implement an explorer/worker role split using pi's fork/spawn session capability: spawn a read-only explorer session at goal-set time to produce a structured task breakdown (with RFC 2119 MUST/SHOULD/MAY verbs and explicit scope boundaries per task), then gate task creation so no new tasks can be added after the planning phase closes. This prevents scope creep during execution and ensures the task breakdown quality is determined upfront with full codebase context, rather than incrementally discovered mid-execution.

area: Claude Code on-task persistence mechanisms: TodoWrite/TaskCreate, Plan Mode, Stop hooks, subagents (Task/Agent tool), CLAUDE.md/auto-memory, and the /goal command

mechanisms.name: TodoWrite / TaskCreate-TaskUpdate lifecycle
mechanisms.whatItIs: Claude Code embeds a task-list tool (originally TodoWrite, superseded by TaskCreate/TaskUpdate/TaskList/TaskGet in v2.1.142+) that Claude is instructed—via its system prompt tool description—to use proactively for any work requiring 3 or more steps. The tool enforces a three-state lifecycle: pending → in_progress → completed. The behavioral rules baked into the tool description are explicit: exactly ONE task may be in_progress at any time; a task must be marked in_progress BEFORE work begins; a task must NEVER be marked completed if tests are failing, the implementation is partial, errors are unresolved, or required files are missing. Tasks must be marked completed immediately after finishing, not batched. The TaskUpdate description (ccVersion 2.1.173) adds dependency fields (addBlocks, addBlockedBy) enabling explicit sequencing between tasks, so a downstream step is held pending until its blocker resolves.
mechanisms.evidence: Full tool descriptions fetched from github.com/Piebald-AI/claude-code-system-prompts (ccVersion 2.1.84 for TodoWrite, ccVersion 2.1.173 for TaskUpdate). Official SDK docs at code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/todo-tracking confirm the lifecycle and migration path. The exact rule: 'ONLY mark a task as completed when you have FULLY accomplished it.'
mechanisms.applicability: pi-goal already has a goal_task todo tool persisted in SQLite. The key upgrades from this mechanism are: (1) enforce the one-in-progress-at-a-time invariant in the tool schema so the agent cannot mark two tasks active simultaneously; (2) add a blockedBy dependency field so the task breakdown can encode sequencing (e.g., 'run tests' blocks 'mark feature complete'); (3) mirror Claude's rule that tasks stay in_progress until tests pass—pi-goal's tool_result hook can reject a completion call if it detects failing tests in the recent shell output.

mechanisms.name: Stop Hook completion gate with stop_hook_active loop guard
mechanisms.whatItIs: A Stop hook is a callback registered for the agent lifecycle event that fires when Claude finishes generating a response. The hook receives a JSON payload including the transcript path and a boolean field stop_hook_active. Returning exit code 2 (or JSON {decision: 'block', reason: '...'}) prevents Claude from stopping; the reason string becomes Claude's next instruction. The stop_hook_active flag is the critical loop-prevention mechanism: when it is true, a prior block on this turn has already fired, so the hook must exit 0 immediately to allow eventual stopping. Stop hooks can also inject additionalContext (non-blocking) instead of hard-blocking, providing feedback without forcing continuation. The morphllm.com and amitkoth.com references document the exact blocking/non-blocking distinction and the pattern of running a lightweight evaluator (Haiku) against the transcript to produce a specific, actionable reason string.
mechanisms.evidence: Official hook schema documented at code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/hooks and code.claude.com/docs/en/hooks. The stop_hook_active field is visible in the SubagentStop hook example in the SDK docs: 'console.log(`Stop hook active: ${subInput.stop_hook_active}`)'. The system prompt for the stop-condition evaluator (agent-prompt-hook-condition-evaluator-stop.md, ccVersion 2.1.143) contains the exact JSON response schema. The codingwithroby.substack.com article documents the 'one chance to push back per stretch of work' rule.
mechanisms.applicability: pi-goal's existing COMPLETION GATE pattern (forcing another turn until goal_complete is called) maps directly onto a Stop hook. The upgrades are: (1) read the transcript at hook time and run a lightweight evaluator model against it to produce a specific reason (not a generic 'you haven't finished' message); (2) check stop_hook_active to avoid infinite blocking loops; (3) inject structured evidence requirements into the reason string (e.g., 'your goal_complete call is missing verifications_run—run the test suite and report results').

mechanisms.name: Hook condition evaluator (Haiku judge model)
mechanisms.whatItIs: Claude Code v2.1.139 introduced the /goal command, which wires a dedicated lightweight evaluator model (default: Haiku) into the Stop hook. After every agent turn, the evaluator receives the user-defined completion condition (up to 4,000 characters of natural language) and the full conversation transcript. It returns {ok: true, reason: '...'} to allow stopping or {ok: false, reason: '...'} to continue. A third form {ok: false, impossible: true, reason: '...'} signals the goal can never be reached. The evaluator prompt (agent-prompt-hook-condition-evaluator-stop.md) explicitly instructs the judge to quote transcript evidence for its decision rather than accepting the assistant's self-assessment: 'the assistant claiming the goal is impossible is evidence, not proof.' The companion agent-prompt-hook-condition-evaluator.md (for non-stop hooks) is even simpler—a single-call JSON judge without the impossible state.
mechanisms.evidence: agent-prompt-hook-condition-evaluator-stop.md fetched via GitHub API (ccVersion 2.1.143). The /goal command architecture described at help.apiyi.com/en/claude-code-goal-mode-keep-working-until-done-guide-en.html. The four-step evaluation loop (context packaging → model decision → routing → UI refresh) is documented there.
mechanisms.applicability: pi-goal already has a COMPLETION GATE that forces another turn. Replacing the gate's internal logic with a Haiku judge call against the transcript gives structured, evidence-grounded rejection reasons. The judge prompt can be parameterized with pi-goal's structured-evidence requirements (requirements_covered, verifications_run, task_evidence, shortcuts_considered) so the rejection message tells the agent exactly which fields are missing or unsubstantiated.

mechanisms.name: Plan Mode (read-only exploration before execution)
mechanisms.whatItIs: Plan Mode is a permission mode where Claude is STRICTLY PROHIBITED from creating, modifying, or deleting files. Its sole job is to read files, trace code paths, understand architecture, identify existing patterns, and produce a step-by-step implementation plan with a 'Critical Files for Implementation' section listing 3-5 key files. The system prompt (agent-prompt-plan-mode-enhanced.md) enforces this by prohibiting writing at the prompt level, not just via permissions. The four-step process is: understand requirements → explore thoroughly → design solution → detail the plan. Plan Mode integrates with TaskCreate in v2.1.84+: 'When using plan mode, create a task list to track the work.'
mechanisms.evidence: agent-prompt-plan-mode-enhanced.md, described by fetched content from github.com/Piebald-AI/claude-code-system-prompts. The tool descriptions tool-description-enterplanmode.md and tool-description-exitplanmode.md are present in the repository (ccVersion visible in directory listing). The TaskCreate tool description (ccVersion 2.1.84) explicitly mentions plan mode integration.
mechanisms.applicability: pi-goal can adopt a planning phase by injecting a 'you are in planning mode, do not write code yet' constraint into the goal_state reminder at the start of a session, then switching to execution mode once the task list is confirmed. This separates scope-setting from execution and reduces the agent diving into the wrong subtask first.

mechanisms.name: Subagent orchestration via Worker Fork and scope isolation
mechanisms.whatItIs: Claude Code spawns subagents using the Agent tool (formerly Task tool). Two key patterns exist: (1) Worker Fork—a subagent that inherits the parent's full context but executes ONE directive and stops, governed by 'Do NOT spawn subagents' and 'report once and stop'; (2) fresh general-purpose agents that start with a blank context and a specialized system prompt. Workers are capped at maxTurns: 200, have access to all tools (tools: *), and use permissionMode: 'bubble' (escalating permission requests to the parent). The SubagentStop hook fires when any worker finishes, providing agent_id, agent_transcript_path, and stop_hook_active for result aggregation. The agent-prompt-code-review-part-4 three-state verification system shows a concrete adversarial pattern: a reviewer finds issues, a separate verifier agent classifies each as CONFIRMED, PLAUSIBLE, or REFUTED by quoting the code.
mechanisms.evidence: agent-prompt-worker-fork.md fetched via GitHub API (ccVersion 2.1.169, shows maxTurns: 200, tools: *, permissionMode: bubble). agent-prompt-code-review-part-4-three-state-verification-phase.md (ccVersion 2.1.173) shows the CONFIRMED/PLAUSIBLE/REFUTED schema. SubagentStop hook example in code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/hooks shows agent_transcript_path field.
mechanisms.applicability: pi-goal can use its fork/spawn session capability to spawn a verification subagent after the main agent calls goal_complete. The verifier reads the transcript and checks each structured-evidence field against actual file contents or test output. The three-state schema (CONFIRMED/PLAUSIBLE/REFUTED) maps directly onto pi-goal's required fields: a verifier can classify each requirement as confirmed (test output shows it passing), plausible (agent claimed it but no test was run), or refuted (code search shows the requirement was not implemented).

mechanisms.name: CLAUDE.md always-loaded context and auto-memory
mechanisms.whatItIs: CLAUDE.md files are injected in full into every session's context window at launch, in load order from broadest to most specific scope (managed policy → user → project → local). The project-root CLAUDE.md survives /compact: after compaction Claude re-reads it from disk and re-injects it. Auto memory (enabled by default since v2.1.59) lets Claude write its own notes to ~/.claude/projects/<project>/memory/MEMORY.md; the first 200 lines or 25KB of MEMORY.md are loaded at session start. Path-scoped .claude/rules/ files load only when Claude opens matching files, reducing noise. The key design principle documented: 'CLAUDE.md content is delivered as a user message after the system prompt, not as part of the system prompt itself'—meaning it is context that shapes behavior, not hard enforcement.
mechanisms.evidence: Full memory documentation at code.claude.com/docs/en/memory. The compaction survival behavior is explicitly stated: 'Project-root CLAUDE.md survives compaction: after /compact, Claude re-reads it from disk and re-injects it.' The 200-line/25KB MEMORY.md limit and the 'user message after system prompt' delivery mechanism are from the same source.
mechanisms.applicability: pi-goal injects a <goal_state> reminder before every LLM call. The CLAUDE.md mechanism confirms this is the right delivery channel (post-system-prompt user message), but also reveals a risk: if the injected block is too large or injected on every turn regardless of compaction, it wastes tokens and can reduce adherence. The upgrade is to keep goal_state concise (active tasks + next action only), persist the full goal+task state in SQLite (as pi-goal already does), and re-inject from SQLite after compaction events via the PreCompact/PostCompact hooks.

mechanisms.name: UserPromptSubmit hook for per-turn context injection
mechanisms.whatItIs: The UserPromptSubmit hook fires after the user presses Enter and before the model receives the prompt. It can return additionalContext inside hookSpecificOutput, which is delivered as a system reminder alongside the prompt—not as a chat message visible in the UI. This is the mechanism for injecting dynamic per-turn context: current branch, failing tests, open tasks, goal state. The hook can also block the prompt entirely (exit 2) or allow it through unchanged. A critical constraint: the hook cannot rewrite the prompt text itself, only append context. The hidekazu-konishi.com reference documents that plain-text stdout (as opposed to JSON) from UserPromptSubmit and UserPromptExpansion hooks is also injected into context, giving shell command hooks a simpler path for basic injection.
mechanisms.evidence: code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/hooks documents the additionalContext field for UserPromptSubmit. The morphllm.com hooks reference documents the exact JSON shape for the hookSpecificOutput. The github.com/thedotmack/claude-mem issue #1079 shows a real example of a UserPromptSubmit hook injecting a security guidance block as a system reminder every turn.
mechanisms.applicability: pi-goal already injects <goal_state> before every LLM call. Mapping this to a UserPromptSubmit hook (or its equivalent in pi's extension API) makes the injection dynamic: the hook reads from SQLite, formats only the tasks that are pending or in_progress, and appends the current goal's completion condition. This avoids token waste from injecting the full history of completed tasks every turn.

mechanisms.name: PostToolUse hook for inline test/lint steering
mechanisms.whatItIs: The PostToolUse hook fires after a tool executes successfully. It can return additionalContext that is appended to the tool result Claude receives, or it can return updatedToolOutput to replace the tool result entirely. Because the tool has already run, this hook cannot undo the action, but it can inject immediate feedback that steers the next action. A common pattern is running ESLint or a targeted test suite against the edited file immediately after an Edit/Write tool call, then appending the output to the tool result so Claude sees the failure before it moves to the next task. The PostToolBatch variant fires once after an entire parallel tool batch resolves, making it suitable for batch consistency checks.
mechanisms.evidence: code.claude.com/docs/en/agent-sdk/hooks documents additionalContext and updatedToolOutput for PostToolUse. The hidekazu-konishi.com complete guide shows the PostToolBatch pattern for parallel tool validation. The morphllm.com reference provides the full JSON schema for PostToolUse hookSpecificOutput.
mechanisms.applicability: pi-goal can use PostToolUse on Write/Edit tool calls to immediately run targeted tests against the changed file and inject results into the tool result. If tests fail, the agent sees the failure as part of the same turn and corrects before moving to the next task—rather than discovering failures only at the COMPLETION GATE. This converts the gate from a single end-of-run checkpoint into continuous steering pressure throughout the run.

mapsToPiGoal:
1. Replace pi-goal's blunt COMPLETION GATE (loop until goal_complete is called) with a Stop-hook Haiku judge that reads the transcript and evaluates each structured-evidence field (requirements_covered, verifications_run, task_evidence, shortcuts_considered) against observable evidence, returning a specific rejection reason that names which field is missing and what evidence would satisfy it. Wire the stop_hook_active flag to prevent infinite blocking. This gives the agent actionable, targeted feedback instead of a generic 'you have not finished' wall.

2. Add continuous PostToolUse steering on Write/Edit calls: immediately run targeted tests/lint against the changed file and inject results into the tool result via additionalContext. This converts quality enforcement from a single end-of-run checkpoint into per-edit pressure, so the agent corrects failures in the same turn they occur rather than accumulating debt that the completion gate must reject.

3. Adopt the Worker Fork pattern for verification: after the main agent calls goal_complete, spawn a read-only verification subagent (no write tools, short maxTurns) that independently checks each requirement against file contents and test output, classifying each as CONFIRMED, PLAUSIBLE, or REFUTED with a transcript quote. Only allow stopping if all requirements are CONFIRMED. This separates the agent that does the work from the agent that audits it, preventing self-certification bias.

mechanisms.name: .cursor/rules MDC Rule System (Four Application Modes)
mechanisms.whatItIs: Project rules live in .cursor/rules as .mdc files with YAML frontmatter that controls when they apply. There are four modes: Always (alwaysApply: true — injected into every context), Auto-Attached (globs field — injected whenever a matching file is in context), Agent-Requested (description field only — the model reads the description and decides whether to pull the rule in), and Manual (@-mention). Agent-Requested rules are especially powerful: the model semantically decides relevance, so rules can encode conditional expertise (e.g., a 'testing standards' rule that only surfaces when test files are touched). Rules are version-controlled in the repo and team-shared. Plain .md files in .cursor/rules are silently ignored — only .mdc with frontmatter works.
mechanisms.evidence: Cursor official docs at https://cursor.com/docs/rules: 'Agent reads the description and pulls the rule in when relevant.' 'Plain .md files are ignored because they lack frontmatter.' Rule hierarchy: Team Rules > Project Rules > User Rules.
mechanisms.applicability: pi-goal can inject a high-quality 'goal standards' rule via resources_discover, contributing an Agent-Requested .mdc skill/prompt file. The model will pull it in only when the goal is active. More specifically: task-breakdown discipline, test/lint requirements, and scope-enforcement prose can live in dedicated rule files with targeted glob patterns (e.g., auto-attach to *.test.ts to enforce TDD) rather than being crammed into the system prompt every turn.

mechanisms.name: Cursor Memories — Background Proposal + Approval Flow
mechanisms.whatItIs: Introduced in Cursor v0.51 / v1.0 (June 2025), Memories are per-project facts extracted from chat by a background model. The background model proposes a memory; the user approves it before it is saved. Once approved, the memory is injected into future sessions automatically. The toggle is at Cursor Settings → Rules → 'Generate Memories'. Memories are stored at the project level (not global), can be reviewed and deleted from Settings, and are conceptually auto-generated rules managed by the settings system rather than .mdc files. The feature was later removed in Cursor 2.1.x but the pattern it established (background model watches session, proposes durable facts) persists in the continual-learning plugin.
mechanisms.evidence: Cursor changelog for v1.0 (https://cursor.com/changelog/1-0): 'Memories are stored per project on an individual level, and can be managed from Settings.' Forum thread https://forum.cursor.com/t/0-51-memories-feature/98509 confirmed the propose-then-approve flow. MemNexus blog (https://memnexus.ai/blog/2026-02-20-cursor-persistent-memory) notes the feature was removed in 2.1.x.
mechanisms.applicability: The propose-then-approve pattern maps directly to a pi-goal improvement: at agent_end (or on goal_complete), an LLM call can mine the session transcript for durable facts (reusable task patterns, recurring mistakes, codebase conventions the agent discovered), propose them to the user, and if approved append them as bullet points to AGENTS.md. This creates a ratchet: each goal session leaves the workspace smarter for the next one.

mechanisms.name: Continual-Learning Stop-Hook Plugin (cursor/plugins)
mechanisms.whatItIs: The official cursor/plugins repo contains a continual-learning plugin that watches agent sessions and incrementally updates AGENTS.md. It has three components: (1) a stop hook that fires on every agent session end and checks whether learning conditions are met (default: 10+ turns completed and 120+ minutes since last run, with a trial mode of 3 turns / 15 minutes); (2) a continual-learning skill that, when the stop hook emits a followup_message, orchestrates the update workflow; and (3) an agents-memory-updater subagent that reads only new or changed transcript files (tracked by a secondary index JSON), reads existing AGENTS.md first to avoid duplication, and writes plain bullet points in-place. State is persisted in two JSON files: .cursor/hooks/state/continual-learning.json (cadence: lastRunAtMs, turnsSinceLastRun, lastTranscriptMtimeMs, lastProcessedGenerationId, trialStartedAtMs) and .cursor/hooks/state/continual-learning-index.json (incremental transcript index). The local repo already has a continual-learning.json with lastRunAtMs=0 and turnsSinceLastRun=5, meaning it was installed but has not triggered yet.
mechanisms.evidence: Cursor plugins repo at https://github.com/cursor/plugins/tree/main/continual-learning. Local file /Users/mish/.pi/agent/extensions/pi-goal-extension/.cursor/hooks/state/continual-learning.json contains {version:1, lastRunAtMs:0, turnsSinceLastRun:5, lastProcessedGenerationId:'2ad758aa-ff49-442a-9c66-d87789564472', trialStartedAtMs:null}. DeepWiki summary at https://deepwiki.com/microsoft/agent-skills/5.9-hooks-and-continual-learning describes the agents-memory-updater and its transcript-delta strategy.
mechanisms.applicability: The stop hook's followup_message mechanism maps exactly to pi-goal's agent_end hook. pi-goal already implements a one-shot completion gate via agent_end; the same pattern can trigger a background AGENTS.md update after goal_complete fires. The cadence check (turnsSinceLastRun, elapsed time) prevents thrashing. The incremental transcript-delta strategy keeps cost low. Adapting this to pi-goal means: on goal completion, spawn a subagent that reads only the transcript since goal start, extracts task patterns and codebase facts, and appends them to AGENTS.md as scoped bullet points.

mechanisms.name: Cursor Stop Hook with followup_message — Iterative Agent Loop Control
mechanisms.whatItIs: Cursor hooks (introduced v1.7, October 2025) execute shell scripts that receive JSON via stdin and return JSON via stdout. The stop hook fires when an agent session ends and receives {status: 'completed'|'aborted'|'error', loop_count: number}. When the hook returns a followup_message string, Cursor automatically submits it as the next user message, triggering another agent turn. This creates a controlled re-entry loop without user intervention. A configurable loop_limit (default 5, overridable per hook, or null for unlimited) prevents infinite loops; loop_count in the input payload lets the hook implement conditional exit logic. The subagentStop hook has the same followup_message mechanic and additionally receives structured metadata: status, task summary, duration_ms, message_count, modified_files[], and agent_transcript_path.
mechanisms.evidence: Cursor official docs at https://cursor.com/docs/hooks — full hook schema with all fields and return values confirmed. The agent-best-practices blog (https://cursor.com/blog/agent-best-practices) explicitly shows 'Configure .cursor/hooks.json with scripts that automatically trigger follow-up actions. Example: keep agent working until tests pass by returning followup_message from hook scripts.'
mechanisms.applicability: pi-goal already implements the conceptual equivalent of this (agent_end fires a continuation via sendUserMessage with deliverAs:'followUp'), but the Cursor stop hook's loop_count gives a clean way to implement escalation tiers: pass 0 = run tests and report; pass 1 = fix failures; pass 2 = escalate to senior model. pi-goal can replicate this pattern using its own agent_end hook combined with ctx.getContextUsage() and pi.setThinkingLevel() to progressively raise thinking level on each retry.

mechanisms.name: preToolUse Hook — Tool Call Interception and Modification
mechanisms.whatItIs: The preToolUse hook fires before any tool executes and receives {tool_name, tool_input, tool_use_id, cwd, agent_message}. It can return: permission ('allow'/'deny'/'ask'), user_message (injected into the human turn), agent_message (injected into the model context), and updated_input (a modified version of the tool's input). This enables deterministic, code-enforced policies at the tool boundary: block dangerous operations, silently rewrite tool parameters (e.g., redirect file writes to a staging area), or inject advisory context without requiring the model to proactively include it. The postToolUse hook receives {tool_name, tool_input, tool_output, duration} and can return additional_context to inject into the next model context — enabling tool-output post-processing or annotation.
mechanisms.evidence: Full schema confirmed from Cursor docs at https://cursor.com/docs/hooks. The preToolUse updated_input return field and postToolUse additional_context field are both in the official spec.
mechanisms.applicability: pi-goal's tool_call and tool_result hooks are the direct equivalent. The Cursor preToolUse pattern of injecting agent_message at the tool boundary maps to pi-goal's ability to modify tool results. Concretely: intercept bash/shell tool calls to enforce that test commands are run before goal_complete is allowed; intercept file-write tool calls to annotate them to the task tracker; use postToolUse/tool_result to automatically run a linter after any file edit and inject the lint output into the next turn's context. This is 'test/lint as steering pressure' — the agent sees the feedback inline without a separate task.

mechanisms.name: Bugbot Learned Rules — Signal-Driven Rule Generation from PR Feedback
mechanisms.whatItIs: Bugbot (Cursor's automated PR reviewer, shipped in July 2025) implements a continual self-improvement loop. Signals are collected from merged PRs: downvotes on Bugbot comments ('this finding wasn't useful'), developer replies correcting the suggestion, and human reviewer comments flagging issues Bugbot missed. These signals are processed into candidate rules that are evaluated against incoming PRs. A candidate rule transitions to 'active' when it accumulates supporting evidence; active rules with consistent negative feedback are disabled. Rules are stored per-repo and function as supplementary reviewer instructions customized to each codebase's business context. As of early 2026, over 110,000 repos have enabled learning and generated 44,000+ rules; Bugbot's bug resolution rate went from 52% to near 80% since launch.
mechanisms.evidence: Cursor blog post 'Bugbot now self-improves with learned rules' at https://cursor.com/blog/bugbot-learning: 'Since launching learned rules in beta, more than 110,000 repos have enabled learning, generating more than 44,000 learned rules.' Resolution rate improvement from 52% to ~80% is stated in the same post.
mechanisms.applicability: pi-goal's completion gate captures structured evidence for every goal (requirementsCovered, verificationsRun, shortcutsConsidered). This is an untapped signal source. A background learner that reads completed goals' evidence fields could extract patterns like 'agent consistently skips integration tests for this codebase' or 'agent marks tasks complete before running tsc' and codify them as new rules appended to AGENTS.md or as tighter field-level descriptions in GoalCompleteParams. This closes the loop: each completed goal makes the gate smarter for the next one.

mechanisms.name: Orchestrate Plugin — Planner/Worker/Verifier Subagent Fan-Out
mechanisms.whatItIs: The official cursor/plugins Orchestrate plugin decomposes a large goal into a tree of parallel cloud agents: a Planner agent produces a structured task graph, Worker agents execute individual tasks on isolated branches, and Verifier agents validate the output of each worker before results are merged. Agents communicate via structured handoffs written to disk (not via shared context), and a reconciliation script merges the tree from disk and git. This is invoked explicitly via /orchestrate <goal>. The subagentStart/subagentStop hooks fire around each subagent, allowing the parent to receive structured summaries including modified_files[], message_count, duration_ms, and agent_transcript_path.
mechanisms.evidence: Cursor marketplace entry for Orchestrate at https://cursor.com/marketplace/cursor/orchestrate: 'fans a large task out across parallel Cursor cloud agents via the Cursor SDK: planners publish tasks, workers hand off back up, and a script reconciles the tree from disk and git.' The subagentStop hook schema is confirmed in the Cursor hooks docs at https://cursor.com/docs/hooks.
mechanisms.applicability: pi-goal's fork/spawn/navigateTree session API is the pi equivalent of subagent fan-out. For complex goals, pi-goal could auto-decompose into a planner subagent (produces a structured task list written back via goal_task calls) and worker subagents (one per major task, with their own goal_state injections and completion gates). The parent extension monitors subagentStop-equivalent events and aggregates evidence before allowing goal_complete on the top-level goal. This enables specialised subagent workflows as listed in the improvement brief.

mechanisms.name: Feedback-Driven Rule Patching via CI — Mid-Session and Post-Merge Rule Updates
mechanisms.whatItIs: A pattern documented by the Elementor engineering team at Medium: a CI workflow runs after every merged PR. It retrieves all human reviewer comments via the GitHub API, feeds them to the Cursor CLI with an extraction prompt, and the agent generates or patches rules in .cursor/rules/code-review.mdc. The patch enforces a 120-line cap by merging similar rules, removing stale ones, and keeping specific beats vague. A /review slash command inside the IDE reads the freshly updated rule file before a PR is submitted, closing the feedback loop within the same session. The key constraint found in practice: vague extraction prompts produce unusable rules; demanding concrete WHAT/HOW/WHY structure is required.
mechanisms.evidence: Medium post by Elementor Engineers at https://medium.com/elementor-engineers/the-self-learning-code-review-teaching-ai-cursor-to-learn-from-human-feedback-454df64c98cc: 'The hardest part was getting the agent to produce useful output. Vague prompts yielded unusable results; demanding specificity transformed extraction quality.' The three-field rule template (WHAT, HOW, WHY) is from the same post.
mechanisms.applicability: pi-goal can run a similar extraction after goal_complete: mine the completed goal's evidence fields and session transcript, extract codebase-specific patterns into structured bullets (WHAT: the rule; WHERE: file/path scope; EVIDENCE: what session data supports it), and append them to AGENTS.md under a 'Learned from goal sessions' section. The 120-line cap / merge-similar-rules discipline prevents AGENTS.md bloat. The quality constraint (demand WHAT/HOW/WHY, not summaries) should be baked into the extraction prompt.

mapsToPiGoal:
Three highest-leverage mappings to pi-goal quality improvement:

1. Continual-learning stop-hook pattern applied to goal completion: The cursor/plugins continual-learning plugin proves the exact pattern pi-goal needs — a stop/agent_end hook that (a) checks a cadence gate using persistent JSON state (already present in this repo at .cursor/hooks/state/continual-learning.json with turnsSinceLastRun=5), (b) emits a followup_message/sendUserMessage to trigger one more agent turn, and (c) in that turn spawns an agents-memory-updater subagent that processes only the transcript delta since the last run and appends plain bullet points to AGENTS.md. Adapting this means pi-goal's completed goals progressively enrich AGENTS.md with codebase-specific facts, raising the quality baseline for every subsequent session without human intervention.

2. Tool-boundary steering via preToolUse/tool_call interception: The Cursor preToolUse hook's ability to inject agent_message and updated_input at the tool boundary maps directly to pi-goal's tool_call hook. The key insight from Cursor's best-practices doc is that 'test/lint as steering pressure' is most reliable when it is injected as tool-output context rather than upfront prompting. pi-goal should intercept bash/shell tool executions, and after any file-write use pi.exec() to run tsc/bun test/lint on the changed files and inject the output as additional context in the tool_result. The agent sees red output immediately after the edit and self-corrects before the next LLM call, without needing a separate verification step or a stronger completion gate.

3. Signal-driven AGENTS.md patching from completion evidence: The Bugbot learned-rules system and the Elementor CI pattern both show that the highest-quality rule improvements come from mining structured signals — not free-form transcripts. pi-goal already captures exactly those signals in the goal_complete evidence schema (requirementsCovered, verificationsRun, shortcutsConsidered). A post-completion background pass that extracts patterns from these fields — specifically recurring shortcuts taken, verifications skipped, and task patterns — and writes them back as AGENTS.md bullets using a WHAT/WHERE/EVIDENCE template would create a true feedback ratchet: each completed goal makes the gate smarter and the agent more calibrated for the next goal on this codebase.
